questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'She will come to the party _____ she finishes her assignment.'

options.option_text: unless
if
although
because

questions.explanation: 'If' introduces a positive condition — 'she comes' only under the condition that she finishes. 'Unless' introduces a negative condition (= 'if not'). 'Although' = despite / even though. 'Because' = cause (answers 'why?'). Test the logic — here coming depends on finishing, so 'if'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the sentence with the correct correlative pair.

options.option_text: Neither he or his brother is here.
Neither he nor his brother is here.
Either he nor his brother is here.
Neither he and his brother is here.

questions.explanation: Fixed correlative pairs — 'neither…nor', 'either…or', 'not only…but also', 'both…and', 'whether…or'. Mixing them (neither…or, either…nor) is ungrammatical. Verb agreement — with 'neither A nor B', verb agrees with the noun closer to it — here 'his brother' (singular) → 'is'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'He ran fast, _____ he missed the bus.'

options.option_text: and
but
so
or

questions.explanation: The two clauses contrast — running fast should have let him catch the bus, yet he missed it. 'But' marks that contrast. 'And' — mere addition. 'So' — cause leading to result. 'Or' — alternative. Use 'but' / 'yet' / 'however' for contrast, 'and' / 'moreover' for addition, 'so' / 'therefore' for consequence.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Walk fast, _____ you will miss the train.'

options.option_text: unless
or
and
but

questions.explanation: An imperative + 'or' states the negative consequence if the command is not obeyed — 'Walk fast, or (else) you will miss the train' = 'If you don't walk fast, you'll miss the train.' 'Unless' would need rephrasing of the first clause. 'And' would mean the walking itself causes the missing, which is wrong here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'no sooner … than'?

options.option_text: No sooner he arrived than the rain started.
No sooner had he arrived than the rain started.
No sooner he had arrived than the rain started.
No sooner he did arrive than the rain started.

questions.explanation: After 'No sooner' (and 'Hardly', 'Scarcely', 'Seldom') at the start of a sentence, the auxiliary is inverted to before the subject — 'No sooner HAD he arrived…'. The second clause uses 'than' (not 'when'). Pair — 'Hardly had he arrived when the rain started.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: '_____ he was very tired, he continued to work.'

options.option_text: Because
Although
So that
Since

questions.explanation: The two clauses are in contrast — being tired should stop work, yet he kept working. 'Although' / 'though' / 'even though' — introduce a contrasting subordinate clause. 'Because' / 'since' — cause (reason). 'So that' — purpose. Never pair 'although' with 'but' in formal writing — 'Although it was raining, he went out' (not '…, but he went out').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence with 'not only … but also'.

options.option_text: She not only sings but also dance.
She not only sings but also dances.
She not only sing but also dances.
She not only sings but also dancing.

questions.explanation: 'Not only … but also' requires parallel structure on both sides. If 'sings' (verb + s) follows 'not only', then 'dances' (matching form) must follow 'but also'. Options A, C, D break parallelism with 'dance' / 'sing' / 'dancing'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that correctly uses 'either...or' with proper subject-verb agreement.

options.option_text: Either the principal or the teachers has to attend the seminar.
Either the principal or the teachers have to attend the seminar.
Either the principal and the teachers have to attend the seminar.
Either the principal nor the teachers have to attend the seminar.

questions.explanation: B is correct: with 'either...or', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. 'Teachers' (plural) is nearer, so 'have' is correct. Option A wrongly matches the verb with 'principal' (singular → 'has'). Option C misuses 'and' instead of 'or', breaking the correlative pair. Option D uses 'nor', which pairs only with 'neither', not 'either'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'so...that' to express degree and result?

options.option_text: The soup was such hot that she could not taste it properly.
The soup was very hot that she could not taste it properly.
The soup was so hot that she could not taste it properly.
The soup was too hot that she could not taste it properly.

questions.explanation: C is correct: the pattern 'so + adjective + that' expresses degree leading to a result. Option A is wrong because 'such' must precede 'a/an + adjective + noun' (e.g., 'such a hot soup that...'). Option B is wrong because 'very...that' is not a recognised conjunction construction. Option D is wrong because 'too' pairs with 'to' (infinitive), not with 'that'.

questions.stem: Identify the grammatically correct sentence using 'hardly' or 'scarcely' as a negative adverb with an appropriate conjunction.

options.option_text: Scarcely had she entered the hall than the lights went out.
Hardly had she entered the hall when the lights went out.
Scarcely she had entered the hall when the lights went out.
Hardly she had entered the hall than the lights went out.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + V3 + when' requires both inversion of subject-auxiliary AND the conjunction 'when'. Option A uses 'than' — this is the error students most commonly make by confusing it with 'no sooner...than'. Option C omits mandatory inversion; 'had' must precede the subject. Option D commits both errors: no inversion and 'than' instead of 'when'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the conjunction 'lest'?

options.option_text: He practised daily lest he would forget the verses by the recital.
He practised daily lest he should forget the verses by the recital.
He practised daily lest he forgets the verses by the recital.
He practised daily lest that he should forget the verses by the recital.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'lest' is a negative purpose conjunction that must be followed by 'should' (subjunctive construction). Option A is wrong because 'lest' never combines with 'would'. Option C is wrong because the bare present tense 'forgets' cannot follow 'lest'. Option D introduces a redundant 'that' after 'lest', which is a frequent written-English error.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'as' functioning as a CAUSAL conjunction (equivalent to 'because'), rather than a temporal one?

options.option_text: As she grew older, her passion for classical music deepened.
As the laboratory was shut, the experiment had to be postponed.
He waved to the crowd as the train pulled slowly out of the station.
As she watched from the terrace, the children played in the rain.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'As the laboratory was shut' states a static condition that causes the result — 'as' = 'because'. Option A uses 'as' temporally (= as time passed / over time). Option C uses 'as' temporally (= at the very moment the train departed). Option D also uses 'as' temporally (= while she was watching). The causal reading is strongest when the 'as' clause describes a state, not a simultaneous action.

questions.stem: Identify the grammatical error in: 'No sooner had the finance minister tabled the budget when the opposition staged a walkout from Parliament.'

options.option_text: 'had' should be replaced with 'has' to reflect the present context.
'tabled' should be replaced with 'table' to keep the verb consistent.
'when' should be replaced with 'than' as 'no sooner' pairs only with 'than'.
'staged' should be replaced with 'had staged' for correct event sequencing.

questions.explanation: C is correct: the fixed correlative is 'no sooner...than' — 'when' is an intrusion from the 'hardly/scarcely...when' pattern and is incorrect here. Option A is wrong: past perfect 'had' is precisely correct in a past-narrative 'no sooner' clause. Option B is wrong: 'tabled' (past participle after 'had') is grammatically sound. Option D is wrong: the simple past 'staged' correctly describes the result event; changing it to 'had staged' would illogically reverse the sequence.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences contains a conjunction-related grammatical error?

options.option_text: Both the captain and the players were felicitated for the championship win.
The director, as well as his deputies, was summoned before the inquiry panel.
Neither the CEO nor the board members was informed about the acquisition deal.
Not only the clerks but also the manager has signed the undertaking document.

questions.explanation: C is incorrect: with 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Board members' is plural and closer to the verb, so it must be 'were informed', not 'was'. Option A is correct: 'both...and' always triggers a plural verb ('were'). Option B is correct: with 'as well as', the verb agrees only with the primary subject 'director' (singular → 'was'). Option D is correct: 'manager' is the nearer subject and is singular, so 'has' is correct.
